lessons.title: Supplementary Lesson: Microorganisms in Action — Useful and Harmful Roles
objectives: Describe useful roles of microorganisms in humans, agriculture, food processing, industry and the environment.
Explain how microorganisms can cause food spoilage, material deterioration and disease.
Distinguish beneficial microorganisms from harmful microorganisms using examples.
lessons.body:
# Microorganisms in Action: Useful and Harmful Roles
**SS 1 Biology · Third Term · Week 2**

> This is an independently written supplement to the school's Week 2 note. It organizes the source's listed beneficial and harmful effects and adds clear examples. It does not replace the original source text.

## Learning objectives
You should be able to describe useful roles of microorganisms, explain harmful effects and distinguish beneficial microbes from pathogens and spoilage organisms.

## 1. Microorganisms are not all harmful
Microorganisms include bacteria, microscopic fungi, protozoans and some other microscopic organisms. Some cause disease or spoil food, but many are harmless or useful. Their effects depend on the organism and where it is found.

## 2. Useful roles of microorganisms

### 2.1 Digestion in animals
Microorganisms in the digestive systems of ruminants such as cattle, sheep and goats help break down cellulose in plant material. The animal benefits from nutrients released during this microbial digestion. Some microorganisms in the human gut also help process food and produce certain vitamins; they do not replace a balanced diet.

### 2.2 Agriculture and soil fertility
- Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead plants, animals and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment.
- Some bacteria, including *Rhizobium* species, live in root nodules of legumes such as beans and cowpea. They convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that can enter the nitrogen cycle.
- Soil microorganisms participate in nutrient cycling and help maintain soil processes.

### 2.3 Food processing
- Selected lactic-acid bacteria are used to ferment milk in yoghurt and some cheeses.
- Yeast is used in bread-making. It produces carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise.
- Selected microorganisms are used to make fermented foods and beverages. Food fermentation must use suitable starter organisms and hygienic methods.

### 2.4 Medicine and biotechnology
Some microorganisms produce substances used to make medicines, including certain antibiotics. Other microorganisms are used in biotechnology to produce enzymes, amino acids, vitamins and organic acids. These are selected industrial strains; not every microorganism can produce these substances.

### 2.5 Waste treatment and environmental cleaning
Microorganisms help break down organic waste in sewage-treatment systems. Certain microbes can also break down or transform some pollutants; this is called **bioremediation**. The process must be designed and monitored by trained specialists.

## 3. Harmful effects of microorganisms

### 3.1 Food spoilage
Some bacteria, yeasts and moulds grow on food and cause undesirable changes such as bad smells, souring, slime, colour changes or visible mould. Spoilage can make food unacceptable and some microbial contamination can make food unsafe. Do not taste food to test whether it is spoiled.

### 3.2 Diseases
Some microorganisms are pathogens that cause disease in humans, animals or plants. Examples include bacteria that cause cholera, viruses that cause measles, fungi that cause ringworm and protozoans that cause malaria. The pathogen and route of transmission differ by disease; correct identification matters.

### 3.3 Damage to materials
Some moulds and bacteria can damage stored food, leather, paper, textiles, wood and other materials, especially where moisture and suitable nutrients are available.

## 4. Useful versus harmful effects — comparison

| Area | Useful role | Possible harmful effect |
|---|---|---|
| Human and animal digestion | Help digest some food materials and support gut functions | Some microbes cause infections |
| Agriculture | Decomposition and nitrogen fixation | Some microbes cause crop or livestock diseases |
| Food | Fermentation of yoghurt, bread and other foods | Food spoilage and foodborne illness |
| Industry and medicine | Production of selected enzymes, acids and antibiotics | Contamination can spoil products |
| Environment | Sewage treatment and breakdown of some pollutants | Some microbes contaminate water or cause disease |

## 5. Important distinctions
- **Decomposition** is the breakdown of dead organic material; it is an important natural process.
- **Fermentation** is a process in which microorganisms obtain energy from organic substances, often producing acids, gases or alcohols.
- **Food spoilage** is deterioration in food quality. Spoilage and food safety are related but not identical: food can be unsafe even when it looks normal.
- **Pathogens** are disease-causing organisms. Most microorganisms are not pathogens.

## 6. Summary
Microorganisms help digestion, recycle nutrients, improve soil fertility, process food, produce useful industrial substances and treat waste. Other microorganisms spoil food, damage materials or cause disease. Their effects depend on the species and conditions.

## 7. Practice questions and marking guide

**Q1 (4 marks):** State four useful roles of microorganisms.
**Answer:** Any four: cellulose digestion in ruminants; decomposition; nitrogen fixation; food fermentation; production of selected antibiotics; production of industrial enzymes; sewage treatment or bioremediation.
**Marking:** one mark for each distinct valid role.

**Q2 (4 marks):** Explain how microorganisms can help improve soil fertility.
**Answer:** Decomposer microbes break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as *Rhizobium* live in legume root nodules and convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that enter the nitrogen cycle.
**Marking:** decomposition/nutrient recycling (2); nitrogen fixation/root-nodule example (2).

**Q3 (4 marks):** Give two examples of microorganisms used in food processing and state their roles.
**Answer:** Yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise; lactic-acid bacteria ferment milk to make yoghurt and some cheeses.
**Marking:** two correct microbe groups (2); correct roles (2).

**Q4 (4 marks):** State four harmful effects of microorganisms.
**Answer:** Food spoilage, diseases in humans, diseases in animals, diseases in plants and deterioration of materials.
**Marking:** any four distinct valid effects.

**Q5 (4 marks):** Distinguish decomposition, fermentation and food spoilage.
**Answer:** Decomposition breaks down dead organic matter; fermentation is microbial energy production from organic substances, often forming acids or gases; food spoilage is undesirable deterioration of food quality.
**Marking:** one correct explanation for each (3); clear distinction between useful fermentation and spoilage (1).

**Q6 (4 marks):** Explain why not all microorganisms should be described as germs that cause disease.
**Answer:** Many microorganisms are beneficial or harmless. They help digestion, recycle nutrients, fix nitrogen, process foods and treat waste; only some are pathogens.
**Marking:** states not all are harmful (1); gives three useful roles (3).

**Total: 24 marks.**

## Further reading
- OpenStax, *Biology 2e*, section 22.5, Beneficial Prokaryotes: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/22-5-beneficial-prokaryotes
- OpenStax, *Biology 2e*, section 22.3, Prokaryotic Metabolism: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/22-3-prokaryotic-metabolism

## Disease examples: corrected reference table

The school source's disease table has a heading row and 20 named disease entries. Some entries use a symptom (diarrhoea) or a broad condition (pneumonia) as though it had one cause. The table below preserves the useful examples but corrects those classifications and updates transmission and prevention. It is for Biology learning, not diagnosis or treatment.

| Disease/example | Causative agent | Common features (not diagnostic by themselves) | Main transmission | Prevention/control principle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chickenpox | Varicella-zoster virus | Fever, tiredness and itchy fluid-filled rash | Respiratory particles and contact with blister fluid | Vaccination where included in the national schedule; avoid exposing others while infectious |
| Cholera | *Vibrio cholerae* bacterium | Watery diarrhoea, vomiting and potentially severe dehydration | Food or water contaminated with faeces | Safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene and prompt clinical care |
| Common cold | Many respiratory viruses; rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause | Sneezing, runny nose, sore throat and cough | Respiratory particles and close contact | Hand hygiene, ventilation and staying home when ill; antibiotics do not treat viral colds |
| Dengue | Dengue virus | Fever, headache, muscle/joint pain and sometimes rash | Infected *Aedes* mosquitoes | Prevent mosquito bites and remove standing-water breeding sites |
| Giardiasis (the source labels this row “Diarrhoea”) | *Giardia duodenalis* protozoan | Diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, gas and fatigue | Faecal–oral spread through contaminated water, food, hands or surfaces | Safe water, sanitation and handwashing |
| Diphtheria | Toxin-producing *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* | Sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands and sometimes a thick throat membrane | Respiratory droplets and close contact | Routine vaccination and prompt public-health/clinical response |
| Leprosy (Hansen disease) | *Mycobacterium leprae* | Skin patches with loss of sensation and peripheral nerve involvement | Prolonged close contact with an untreated case, mainly via respiratory droplets | Early diagnosis and completion of professional treatment; it is not spread by casual contact |
| Measles | Measles virus | Fever, cough, runny nose and widespread rash | Airborne spread and respiratory secretions | Measles vaccination and public-health control |
| Pneumococcal pneumonia (one cause of pneumonia) | *Streptococcus pneumoniae* bacterium | Fever, cough, chest pain and difficulty breathing may occur | Respiratory secretions; carriage can occur without illness | Recommended vaccination, hygiene and prompt clinical assessment |
| Poliomyelitis (polio) | Poliovirus | Often mild or without symptoms; some infections cause weakness or paralysis | Mainly faecal–oral spread, including contaminated food or water | Polio vaccination, sanitation and hand hygiene |
| Rabies | Rabies virus (lyssavirus) | Early fever or unusual sensations near a bite; later neurological illness | Saliva from an infected mammal, usually through a bite or scratch | Vaccinate dogs; any possible exposure requires immediate wound washing and urgent medical assessment |
| Streptococcal sore throat (source: “Septic Sore Throat”) | Group A *Streptococcus* (*Streptococcus pyogenes*) | Sore throat, fever and painful swallowing | Respiratory droplets and close contact | Hand hygiene and clinical testing/treatment when indicated |
| African sleeping sickness | *Trypanosoma brucei* parasites | Fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and later sleep-cycle/neurological changes | Bite of an infected tsetse fly | Reduce tsetse exposure and use public-health vector control |
| Smallpox (historical) | Variola virus | Fever followed by a characteristic progressive rash | Before eradication, mainly prolonged close contact and respiratory droplets | Smallpox was declared eradicated; there has been no naturally occurring case since 1977 |
| Tuberculosis (TB) | *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* bacterium | Persistent cough, fever, weight loss, fatigue and night sweats | Airborne particles from a person with infectious pulmonary TB | Early testing and treatment, ventilation, cough hygiene and recommended vaccination |
| Tetanus | *Clostridium tetani* bacterium | Muscle stiffness and painful spasms | Bacterial spores enter a wound; it is not spread person to person | Tetanus vaccination and proper wound care |
| Typhoid fever | *Salmonella enterica* serovar Typhi | Prolonged fever, headache, weakness and abdominal symptoms | Food or water contaminated with human faeces | Safe water, sanitation, food hygiene and vaccination where recommended |
| Whooping cough (pertussis) | *Bordetella pertussis* bacterium | Repeated coughing fits; a whoop may follow a cough | Respiratory droplets and close contact | Routine vaccination and prompt public-health/clinical management |
| Influenza (flu) | Influenza viruses | Fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and fatigue | Respiratory particles/droplets and contaminated hands/surfaces | Annual vaccination where recommended, ventilation and hand hygiene |
| Malaria | *Plasmodium* parasites; *P. falciparum* is especially important in Africa | Fever, chills and headache; severe disease can affect organs | Bite of an infected female *Anopheles* mosquito | Insecticide-treated nets, vector control and prompt testing/medical treatment |

### Corrections to remember
- **Diarrhoea is a symptom, not one disease.** The school source names *Giardia*; the specific disease is giardiasis.
- **Pneumonia has several possible causes.** *Streptococcus pneumoniae* is one important bacterial cause, not the cause of every pneumonia.
- **The common cold has many viral causes.** Rhinoviruses are the most frequent, but not the only cause.
- **Smallpox is eradicated.** It should be taught as a historical disease, not as a current endemic infection.
- **Tetanus is not transmitted person to person.** Spores enter through contaminated wounds.
- **Rabies exposure is an emergency.** Do not advise self-treatment; urgent medical assessment is required after a potentially risky bite or scratch.

No medicine, dose or treatment regimen is prescribed in this lesson. Disease-specific clinical decisions belong to qualified health professionals.

practice.question: State four useful roles of microorganisms.
practice.answer: Cellulose digestion in ruminants; decomposition; nitrogen fixation; food fermentation; production of selected antibiotics; industrial enzymes; sewage treatment or bioremediation.

practice.question: Explain how microorganisms can help improve soil fertility.
practice.answer: Decomposer microbes break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium live in legume root nodules and convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that enter the nitrogen cycle.

practice.question: Give two examples of microorganisms used in food processing and state their roles.
practice.answer: Yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise; lactic-acid bacteria ferment milk to make yoghurt and some cheeses.

practice.question: State four harmful effects of microorganisms.
practice.answer: Food spoilage, diseases in humans, diseases in animals, diseases in plants and deterioration of materials.

practice.question: Distinguish decomposition, fermentation and food spoilage.
practice.answer: Decomposition breaks down dead organic matter; fermentation is microbial energy production from organic substances, often forming acids or gases; food spoilage is undesirable deterioration of food quality.

practice.question: Explain why not all microorganisms should be described as germs that cause disease.
practice.answer: Many microorganisms are beneficial or harmless. They help digestion, recycle nutrients, fix nitrogen, process foods and treat waste; only some are pathogens.

marking.criterion: States not all microbes are harmful

practice.question: For malaria, cholera, tuberculosis, measles and poliomyelitis, name the causative agent and main route of transmission.
practice.answer: Malaria—Plasmodium parasite—bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito; cholera—Vibrio cholerae bacterium—contaminated food or water; TB—Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacterium—airborne particles; measles—measles virus—airborne/respiratory secretions; polio—poliovirus—mainly faecal–oral spread.

practice.question: State one or two common features and one prevention measure for malaria, cholera, tuberculosis, measles and polio.
practice.answer: Malaria: fever/chills/headache; prevent mosquito bites with nets and vector control. Cholera: watery diarrhoea/vomiting; safe water, sanitation and hand hygiene. TB: persistent cough/fever/weight loss/night sweats; early testing, treatment and ventilation. Measles: fever/cough/runny nose/rash; vaccination. Polio: often mild or no symptoms but can cause paralysis; vaccination and sanitation.

practice.question: List three airborne and three mainly food/water-borne infectious diseases from the examples studied.
practice.answer: Airborne: tuberculosis, measles and influenza. Mainly food/water-borne: cholera, poliomyelitis and typhoid fever. Transmission routes can vary by pathogen and setting.

lessons.title: Supplementary Lesson: Natural Vegetative Propagation
objectives: Define natural vegetative propagation and explain how it produces new plants.
Identify natural vegetative structures including bulbs, corms, rhizomes, stem tubers, runners, suckers, roots and leaf plantlets.
Give accurate examples and distinguish natural from artificial vegetative propagation.
lessons.body:
# Natural Vegetative Propagation
**SS 1 Biology · Second Term · Week 1**

> This supplement expands the natural vegetative propagation structures named in the school source. It complements the separate lesson on artificial methods such as cutting, layering, marcotting, budding and grafting.

## Learning objectives
You should be able to define natural vegetative propagation, identify the plant parts involved, give examples and distinguish natural from artificial methods.

## 1. Meaning
**Vegetative propagation** is a form of asexual reproduction in which a new plant develops from a vegetative part of a parent plant, such as a stem, root or leaf, rather than from a seed.

In **natural vegetative propagation**, the plant produces structures that can grow into new plants without people carrying out a propagation technique. The offspring are usually genetically very similar to the parent.

## 2. Natural methods and structures

### 2.1 Rhizomes
A **rhizome** is a horizontal underground stem with nodes and buds. New shoots and roots can grow from its buds.
**Example:** ginger. The pieces of ginger used as food are rhizomes, not roots.

### 2.2 Corms
A **corm** is a short, swollen underground stem that stores food. Buds can grow into new shoots.
**Examples:** cocoyam and gladiolus. A corm is solid inside; it is not the same as a layered bulb.

### 2.3 Stem tubers
A **stem tuber** is a swollen underground stem that stores food and has buds.
**Example:** potato. The small “eyes” on a potato are buds that can grow into shoots. Yam is also commonly propagated from tuber pieces containing buds.

### 2.4 Bulbs
A **bulb** is an underground storage structure with a short stem surrounded by fleshy storage leaves.
**Examples:** onion and garlic. A bulb can produce a new shoot and roots.

### 2.5 Runners or stolons
A **runner** is a slender stem that grows along the soil surface. At some nodes it forms roots and shoots, which can develop into new plants.
**Example:** strawberry.

### 2.6 Suckers
A **sucker** is a shoot that develops from the base or underground stem of a parent plant. It may later become an independent plant.
**Examples:** banana and plantain produce suckers from their underground stem system.

### 2.7 Root tubers and other roots
Some plants form swollen roots that store food. Buds or shoots can develop from suitable root structures.
**Example:** sweet potato is propagated using pieces of storage root that can produce new shoots under suitable conditions. Do not confuse a sweet-potato storage root with a potato stem tuber.

### 2.8 Leaf plantlets
In some plants, buds develop along the leaf margins and grow into small plantlets.
**Example:** *Bryophyllum* (also called *Kalanchoe* in some references). Plantlets can develop roots and grow into new plants.

## 3. Quick comparison

| Structure | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Rhizome | Horizontal underground stem | Ginger |
| Corm | Short, swollen underground stem | Cocoyam; gladiolus |
| Stem tuber | Swollen underground stem with buds | Potato; yam |
| Bulb | Short stem with fleshy storage leaves | Onion; garlic |
| Runner/stolon | Stem growing along the soil surface | Strawberry |
| Sucker | Shoot arising from the parent plant base | Banana; plantain |
| Storage root | Swollen root used for storage and propagation | Sweet potato |
| Leaf plantlet | Small new plant arising from leaf buds | Bryophyllum |

## 4. Natural and artificial propagation
- **Natural vegetative propagation** happens through structures the plant forms naturally, such as rhizomes, bulbs, runners and suckers.
- **Artificial vegetative propagation** is carried out by people using methods such as cutting, layering, marcotting, budding and grafting.

Both are forms of asexual reproduction. They can preserve desirable characteristics, but large groups of genetically similar plants may also share susceptibility to the same disease or environmental stress.

## 5. Summary
New plants can grow naturally from modified stems, roots or leaves. Identify the structure before naming the example: ginger is a rhizome, potato is a stem tuber, onion is a bulb, strawberry produces runners, banana produces suckers and sweet potato is a storage root.

## 6. Practice questions and marking guide

**Q1 (3 marks):** Define natural vegetative propagation.
**Answer:** It is a form of asexual reproduction in which a new plant grows naturally from a vegetative part of the parent, such as a stem, root or leaf, without a seed.
**Marking:** asexual reproduction (1); vegetative part (1); no seed/artificial technique required (1).

**Q2 (4 marks):** Name the vegetative structures of ginger, potato, onion and strawberry.
**Answer:** Ginger—rhizome; potato—stem tuber; onion—bulb; strawberry—runner/stolon.
**Marking:** one each.

**Q3 (4 marks):** Distinguish a corm, a bulb and a rhizome.
**Answer:** A corm is a short swollen underground stem; a bulb has a short stem surrounded by fleshy storage leaves; a rhizome is a horizontal underground stem with nodes and buds.
**Marking:** one correct definition each (3); one suitable example (1).

**Q4 (4 marks):** State four natural vegetative propagation structures and give an example of each.
**Answer:** Any four: rhizome—ginger; corm—cocoyam; stem tuber—potato; bulb—onion; runner—strawberry; sucker—banana; root tuber—sweet potato; leaf plantlet—Bryophyllum.
**Marking:** one mark for each correct pair.

**Q5 (4 marks):** State two differences between natural and artificial vegetative propagation.
**Answer:** Natural propagation occurs through structures the plant forms itself; artificial propagation uses techniques deliberately carried out by people. Examples of natural methods include runners and bulbs; artificial methods include cutting and grafting.
**Marking:** two clear differences (2); suitable examples (2).

**Q6 (4 marks):** Give two advantages and two possible disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
**Answer:** Advantages: desirable features can be retained; plants may mature sooner than seed-grown plants. Disadvantages: little genetic variation; a disease or environmental stress may affect many similar plants.
**Marking:** two advantages (2); two disadvantages (2).

**Total: 23 marks.**

## Further reading
- OpenStax, *Biology 2e*, section 30.2, Stems: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/30-2-stems
- OpenStax, *Biology*, section 32.3, Asexual Reproduction: https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/32-3-asexual-reproduction

lessons.title: Supplementary Lesson: The Compound Light Microscope
objectives: Identify the main parts of a compound light microscope and state their functions.
Calculate total magnification from eyepiece and objective powers.
Explain safe microscope handling and distinguish optional 100× oil immersion from 40× high-power objectives.
lessons.body:
# The Compound Light Microscope
**SS 1 Biology · First Term · Week 2**

## Learning objectives
Identify the main parts of a compound light microscope, state their functions, calculate total magnification and explain safe handling.

## Main parts and functions
| Part | Function |
|---|---|
| Eyepiece (ocular) | Lens viewed through; commonly 10× |
| Body tube/head | Keeps optical components aligned |
| Revolving nosepiece | Holds and selects objective lenses |
| Objective lenses | Magnify the specimen; common powers are 4×, 10× and 40×; some microscopes also have 100× oil immersion |
| Stage and clips/mechanical stage | Support and position the slide |
| Condenser | Concentrates light on the specimen |
| Iris diaphragm | Regulates the light reaching the specimen |
| Illuminator or mirror | Supplies or directs light through the specimen |
| Coarse-focus knob | Makes large focusing movements, normally at low power |
| Fine-focus knob | Makes small adjustments for a sharper image |
| Arm and base | Support the instrument and allow safe carrying |

## Magnification
**Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.** With a 10× eyepiece, 4×, 10×, 40× and 100× objectives give total magnifications of 40×, 100×, 400× and 1000× respectively.

**Microscope models vary.** Some have a built-in illuminator; older models may use a mirror. Some have a mechanical stage and some use simple clips. The 100× objective is a special oil-immersion lens and is not present on every school microscope. The source's 40× highest objective and the figure's 100× objective can describe different configurations; this lesson explains both rather than silently deleting either.

## Safe handling
Carry the microscope with two hands (arm and base); begin with the lowest-power objective; do not let an objective strike the slide; use fine focus at high power; clean lenses with lens paper; use immersion oil only with a designated oil objective and teacher instruction.

## Summary
The eyepiece and objective lenses magnify the specimen. The stage holds the slide; the condenser and diaphragm control illumination; focus knobs sharpen the image. Total magnification is the product of eyepiece and objective magnifications.

## Further reading
- OpenStax, *Microbiology*, section 2.3, Instruments of Microscopy: https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/2-3-instruments-of-microscopy
- Idaho State University, Compound Microscopes: https://www.isu.edu/biology/biolab/instructor-training/technology/microscopes/

practice.question: State the functions of the eyepiece, objective lens, stage and condenser.
practice.answer: The eyepiece is viewed through and provides magnification; the objective lens magnifies the specimen; the stage supports the slide; the condenser focuses light on the specimen.

practice.question: Calculate total magnification with a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective. What would the total be with a 100× objective?
Distinguish the condenser from the iris diaphragm and the illuminator.
practice.answer: The condenser concentrates light on the specimen; the iris diaphragm controls the amount of light; the illuminator or mirror supplies or directs the light.

practice.question: State four rules for safe microscope handling.
practice.answer: Carry by arm and base; start with low power; avoid lens-slide contact; use fine focus at high power; clean lenses with lens paper; use oil only with a designated 100× objective under instruction. Any four.

lessons.title: Supplementary Lesson: Recognising Living and Non-living Things
objectives: Explain how living things differ from non-living things.
Identify characteristics of life and distinguish autotrophic from heterotrophic nutrition.
Compare typical green plant and animal cells and explain plant responses to stimuli.
lessons.body:
# Recognising Living and Non-living Things
**SS 1 Biology · First Term · Week 1/2**

## Learning objectives
Explain how living things differ from non-living things; identify the characteristics of life; distinguish autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition; compare typical green plants and animals.

## Characteristics of living things
Living organisms carry out life processes. A useful school mnemonic is **MRS GREN**: movement, respiration, sensitivity (response to stimuli), growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition. These processes are considered together; no single visible feature is a reliable test on its own. For example, a seed may appear inactive while alive, and a flame may grow and use oxygen but is not a living organism.

## Nutrition
- **Autotrophic nutrition**: an organism makes organic food from inorganic materials. Green plants commonly do this by photosynthesis.
- **Holophytic nutrition** is the traditional school term for plant-like photosynthetic nutrition. Do not confuse it with **halophytic**, which describes organisms adapted to salty environments.
- **Heterotrophic nutrition**: an organism obtains organic food from other organisms or their products. Animals, fungi and many microorganisms are heterotrophs; it is not restricted to animals.

## Growth and movement
Typical animals show determinate growth: growth usually slows or stops at maturity. Many plants show indeterminate growth because meristems can continue producing new tissues. Plants do respond to stimuli, for example by phototropism and gravitropism; they do not usually move from place to place like most animals.

## Typical plant and animal cell differences
| Feature | Typical green plant cell | Typical animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Cellulose wall usually present | No cell wall |
| Chloroplasts | Present in photosynthetic cells | Absent |
| Vacuole | Often a large permanent central vacuole | Usually smaller temporary vacuoles or none |
| Food reserve | Commonly starch | Commonly glycogen |
| Shape | Often more regular due to wall | Often more flexible/variable |

These are typical comparisons, not universal rules for every cell. Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts, and some plants are parasitic. Fungi are heterotrophs and generally store glycogen.

## Excretion
Excretion is removal of metabolic waste products. Plants do not have kidneys, but they can store, transform or release wastes through vacuoles, leaves, bark, resins, gases and roots. Animals have a range of excretory structures; not all animals have kidneys.

## Practice questions and marking guide
**Q1 (4 marks):** State four characteristics of living things and explain why a flame is not living.
**Answer:** Any four MRS GREN processes. A flame is not made of cells and does not reproduce biologically or maintain life processes as an organism.
**Marking:** four characteristics (2); two valid reasons flame is non-living (2).

**Q2 (4 marks):** Distinguish holophytic and heterotrophic nutrition and give two heterotroph examples that are not animals.
**Answer:** Holophytic nutrition makes organic food by photosynthesis; heterotrophic nutrition obtains organic food from other organisms/products. Examples include fungi and many bacteria/protozoans.
**Marking:** two definitions (2); two examples (2).

**Q3 (4 marks):** Explain why plants should not be described as unable to respond to stimuli.
**Answer:** Plants respond through growth or movement responses such as shoots growing towards light (phototropism) and roots growing with gravity (positive gravitropism); they usually do not locomote from place to place.
**Marking:** states plants respond (1); gives two correct examples (2); distinguishes response from locomotion (1).

**Q4 (5 marks):** State five typical differences between green plant cells and animal cells.
**Answer:** Cellulose wall/chloroplasts/large central vacuole in typical green plant cells; no cell wall/no chloroplasts/small or no vacuoles in typical animal cells; plants commonly store starch and animals glycogen.
**Marking:** five correct paired differences (5).

**Total: 17 marks.**

coverage.objective: Observation, hypothesis and experiment defined, and the parts of an experiment: aim, apparatus/materials, method or procedure, result, conclusion

evidence.explanation: Observation (29) is 'the use of human senses to describe an observation by using the characteristics and properties of material', with the same block pointing on from observation to classification, inference, measurement and identification. Hypothesis (30) is 'a sensible proposal or reasonable assumption or a scientific guess that can be subjected to verification or being tested'. Experiment (31) is 'the process used for testing of hypothesis through experimentation during which data are collected', which defines the thing in terms of itself.

The parts of an experiment are given one line each: AIM (33) 'the purpose for which the experiment is carried out'; APPARATUS//MATERIALS (34) 'the materials that will be used for the experiment'; METHOD or PROCEDURE (35) 'used to describe the details that are required step by step'; RESULT (36) 'the record of what is seen during and after the experiment'; CONCLUSION (37) 'used to finalize the outcome of the whole experiment'. They are numbered (iv)-(viii), continuing the (i)-(iii) of blocks 29-31, so the source presents the parts of an experiment as peers of observation, hypothesis and experiment itself. No experiment, apparatus list, quantity or safety instruction is given anywhere in blocks 13-41; the first experiments with materials in this document are the Week 5 experiments I-V at blocks 714-765, and this item invents none.
